extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, War Department officials, personnel officers, and attorneys advising officers on retirement/disability matters
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and legal standards governing examinations, retiring boards, presidential and departmental action, and the computation and effects of retirement for U.S. military officers and enlisted men. Covers definitions (e.g., "line of duty"), evidentiary standards, board powers and limits, pay/grade consequences, and special statutory schemes (acts of 1890, 1904, 1908–1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — "incident of the service" / "line of duty"
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrases 'incident of the service' and 'line of duty' are defined and explained; they are not synonymous but are closely related in meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The several incidents that make up routine military service collectively constitute the 'line of duty' for pension/retirement purposes; a retiring board may apply either understanding to determine a case (C. 15600, Feb. 24, 1904; 19323, Feb. 24, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for "not in line of duty" findings
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer should not be wholly retired unless the testimony as to the cause of the disability establishes, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the incapacity is not the result of any incident of the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding 'not in line of duty' requires strong proof (O. 12992, July 21, 1902). This is the standard applied when deciding whether retirement benefits (and discretion) apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retiring/examining board findings are recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: The finding of a retiring (or examining) board is in the nature of a recommendation and does not alone effect retirement until approved by the President (or proper executive authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No retirement can be ordered on a board's finding until 'approved by the President' (R. 26, 104, Oct. 1867; C. 22743, Feb. 12, 1908). Approval is required to change status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Presidential disapproval
rubrics_metrics.description: If the President disapproves the findings of a retiring board, the officer's status remains unchanged from before the referral to the board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disapproval by the President leaves the officer on the active list; the board's finding alone does not alter status (C. 22743, Feb. 12, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential discretion on retirements not in line of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: When a board finds incapacity not incident to the service, the President has discretion to retire the officer with three‑fourths pay of rank or to wholly retire him with one year's pay and allowances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretion should favor the officer where disability resulted from an untoward incident or excusable fault; if main cause is inexcusable misconduct or persistent misconduct after warnings, wholly retire the officer (C. 22809, Apr. 24, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: One executive action exhausts Presidential power
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the President has fully exercised the power to approve or disapprove board findings and effect retirement, that action is final and exhausts the President's power as to that case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The board finds facts; the President approves or disapproves; when that power has been once fully exercised it is exhausted (P. 56, 426, Dec. 1892; C. 6671; 11223; 22399).

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased rank on retirement (Ordnance Department)
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer retired while detailed in the Ordnance Department should be retired with additional rank held in that department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If detailed under the pertinent acts, additional rank in Ordnance carries to retirement (C. 25677, Oct. 15 & Dec. 17, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased rank requires vacancy before approval
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer cannot be retired with increased rank after board action unless a vacancy in the higher grade occurs before the President approves the board's finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the vacancy occurs before approval, the officer may be retired with the higher rank; otherwise not (O. 9236, Nov. 7, 1900).

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory authority to retire certain categories
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no authority to retire certain officers (e.g., officers of the Philippine Scouts, officers who contracted disability as contract surgeons) under the retirement statutes cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory limits: officers of Philippine Scouts cannot be placed on retired list for disability as such (O. 14314, Mar. 14, 1903); contract surgeon disabilities likewise not a basis for retired-list placement (C. 15892, Mar. 18, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining/retiring boards are not criminal courts for moral charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Examining and retiring boards should not be treated as courts to try moral delinquents; disciplinary measures for moral unfitness should be handled separately when evidence is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where moral unfitness exists, appropriate disciplinary procedures should be used rather than using retiring/examining boards as tribunals for moral charges (C. 23674, July 31, 1908; 24036, Nov. 8, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer entitled to full hearing on moral qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer accused of moral unfitness in an examining/examining-related process is entitled to full hearing: presence of the officer, counsel if desired, full information of allegations, names of accusers, documentary evidence, opportunity to examine witnesses and introduce evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court of inquiry recommended amending orders to insure these procedural protections in moral-qualification matters (C. 18566, June 22, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical incapacity in line of duty — recovery before retirement bars retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer found physically incapacitated in line of duty recovers before retirement, he cannot legally be retired; a new examination is proper and necessary when recovery is alleged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining board findings of incapacity are not final if recovery occurs prior to retirement; new examination required (O. 1979, Jan. 1896; 18723, Oct. 13, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retiring board powers and limits (sec. 1248 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A retiring board may inquire into and determine facts touching the nature/occasion of a disability and shall have such powers of a court-martial and court of inquiry as necessary to that purpose, but it may not try military offenses as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards have broad investigatory power to determine disability but lack jurisdiction to try criminal military offenses (R. 20, 619, May 1866).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retiring board may examine long‑past disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigation of a retiring board is not subject to the time limitations applicable to courts-martial; it may inquire into disabilities however long since they originated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No statute-of-limitations style time bar restricts retiring boards' investigations (R. 20, 619, May 1866).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board must afford officer the right to be present
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer has the right to be present before the retiring board considering his case; the board should not proceed in his absence unless he has waived the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence is a right; waiver required for proceedings in absence (C. 26756, May 24, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of expert (medical) opinion — not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical or other expert opinions are evidence but neither conclusive nor exclusive; the judicial/inquiring mind is entitled to have the facts before it and weigh expert opinions according to completeness of pertinent facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court should not treat medical opinion as final; different experts may reach different conclusions; opinions have variable weight (7 Op. Atty. Gen., 165).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers waive irregularities by silence
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer makes no objection to the proceedings or rulings of a board, he waives irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to object during proceedings may forfeit appellate objections later (24 Ct. Cls., 205).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict enforcement of procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the evidence before a board is so meager that the Secretary of War cannot determine whether disability is in line of duty, strict enforcement of statutory procedures (e.g., section 1248 R.S.) is required to provide an adequate remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards must gather adequate evidence; courts have required strict adherence to procedural protections to enable Secretary determination (C. 15600, Feb. 24, 1904; 15913; 22743).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recorder duties limited unless directed by board
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 1246–1252 R.S. give the board control over its investigation and furnish a recorder to assist; absent specific directions, recorder duties are limited to summoning witnesses and preparing the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards may vest broader presentation duties in the recorder but must do so expressly (C. 17258, Dec. 19, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minority reports permitted from board members
rubrics_metrics.description: A member (or members) of a retiring board may submit a minority report if he believes it will assist the President in reaching a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minority views are allowed and may be forwarded to the Executive (R. 29401, Jan. 21, 1912).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'active service' in retirement statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Active service' relates to the period between appointment to military office and vacation of that office by death, resignation, dismissal, or retirement; officers are presumed capable unless contrary appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contrary appears, Secretary of War has authority to convene retiring board to inquire into nature and extent of disability (C. 22399; 23200).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retirement requires permanency/incurability of disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Incapacity justifying retirement by reason of physical disability relates to permanent, incurable disease or injury that absolutely disqualifies the officer for duty; curable conditions (even if requiring considerable time) generally do not warrant retirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board should test curability within a reasonable time; if curable within reasonable time, officer should be passed; if incurable within such reasonable time, adverse finding appropriate (C. 11350, Oct. 7, 1901).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Cause' of incapacity excludes moral obliquity and financial integrity inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'cause' of 'incapacity' in section 1249 R.S. does not include moral obliquity; financial matters (e.g., unpaid debts, inability to furnish bond) are beyond the board's jurisdiction to recommend retirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards are limited to health/efficiency issues tied to disability; moral/financial issues are generally improper bases for retirement recommendations (C. 19189; 22399; P. 41, 403, July 1890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board cannot recommend retirement for general inefficiency absent health impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry into an officer's general efficiency is pertinent only to the extent it shows inefficiency results from an impairment of health; sections contemplate existing, not purely prospective or contingent incapacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retirement statutes require actual incapacity; general efficiency critiques without health impairment are insufficient (P. 35, 49, Sept. 1889).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incapacity may be found despite origin in prior volunteer service or enlisted service
rubrics_metrics.description: Incapacity found to have resulted from wounds or disabilities contracted in volunteer service or while the officer was enlisted does not affect authority to retire him under the statutes; commissioned officers may be retired for disability contracted while enlisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board/Secretary can act even if the disabling event pre-dated Regular Army service (R. 26, 104, Oct. 1867; C. 15892, Mar. 22,1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of disabilities recognized for retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical and mental conditions such as heat exhaustion causing melancholia/dementia, chronic Bright's disease, deafness, and valvular heart disease have been grounds for retirement on three‑fourths pay or other appropriate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedential examples illustrate the kinds of permanent medical conditions treated as disabling (C. 12277; 17113; 17177; 17223; 23069).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining boards under Oct. 1, 1890 act — suspension/promotion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act, an officer failing for reasons other than physical 'in line of duty' is suspended from promotion for one year and reexamined; failure on reexamination may result in honorable discharge with one year's pay (if failure due to disability not in line of duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examining board finds physical incapacity not in line of duty, statutory consequences (suspension, reexam, discharge) follow and no executive discretion is available in some cases (C. 22809; 28645).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second examinations and sequence rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examining/retiring process includes multiple examinations, outcomes of first and second examinations determine retirement: e.g., if second exam finds physically not in line of duty, wholly retired; if both find not in line of duty, wholly retired; if medical officer found professionally incapacitated and second exam finds in line of duty, other rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence of findings affects final status; specifics are case-dependent (multiple cited examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural formality — oath of members mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations prescribing the oath for board members are sufficiently mandatory that failure to take oath in prescribed manner may warrant disapproval of proceedings; later swearing does not cure defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict compliance with published general orders re swearing is required (C. 20588, Oct. 25, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval of examining-board report transfers officer to retired list
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examining board convened under the act of Oct. 1, 1890 finds an officer incapacitated, and the finding is approved (and a vacancy exists where relevant), the officer is transferred from active to retired list and the change is beyond Executive power to restore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval and resulting status change are final—Executive cannot restore status once legally accomplished (C. 23136, July 21, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory control for medical promotion examinations (1908–1909 acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations of medical officers for promotion are controlled by the act of April 23, 1908 (as amended Mar. 3, 1909); where a major in Medical Corps is found not qualified professionally, proceedings are referred to a board of review and the statutory course (suspension, reexam, retirement) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board-of-review referral and statutory procedures must be followed in medical-officer promotion cases (C. 23135, Nov. 12, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity or new conditions arising after promotion exam
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer passes an examination for promotion but becomes incurably insane before promotion, the favorable finding does not bind the Department to await promotion; a second physical or a retiring board may be ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent disabling conditions discovered prior to promotion can alter outcome and justify reevaluation (C. 28852, Aug. 14, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphine/opiate habituation and service contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer contracts a morphine habit after medicinal use for service-incurred pain, and acquisition was sufficiently contributed to by incidents of the service, the President may exercise discretion to place the officer on the retired list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habit acquired as result of service-related treatment may be treated sympathetically in exercise of executive discretion (C. 22809, Apr. 16, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retired officers' status and civil office limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Retired officers are in military service (subject to trial by general court-martial), are not discharged, may enter government hospitals for the insane, may be kept in civil court jurisdiction, and may hold civil office (federal elective or appointive) subject to limitations, including salary caps (e.g., $2,500 limitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retired officers retain certain military obligations and benefits and face statutory limitations on civil office-holding (sections and cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay, transportation, subsistence, and benefits rules for retired personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules govern pay (longevity), mileage to home after retirement, transportation to home and subsistence, burial, Soldiers' Home, government hospital access; widows' gratuity and other benefit entitlements have specific limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: widow not entitled to six months' gratuity in some contexts; no authority to transport goods to home; mileage and subsistence rules are specified (multiple citations across text).

rubrics_metrics.name: What service counts for enlisted retirement and special counting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules on what service counts include: fraudulent enlistment exclusions (previous dishonorable/without-honor discharges), counting commissioned service, Philippine Constabulary service not counting as officer service, war service counting double in certain wars, definitions of 'actual service', and natives' Philippine service not counting double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various statutes and cases clarify eligibility and computation of service credit for enlisted retirement (act of Sept. 30, 1890; examples in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination and stoppage of retired status/pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Retired status may be terminated by decease, reenlistment, or discharge; pay may be stopped to recoup overpayments or reimburse post-exchange funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative actions may halt pay or terminate status per statutory/regulatory provisions (text examples).
